title: Larkspur overview
text:
# Larkspur overview

Larkspur is an open-source distributed task queue and job scheduler. Applications enqueue tasks over a REST API or an SDK, and a pool of workers executes them with retries, priorities and rate limits.

## Core concepts

A task is a named unit of work with a JSON payload. Tasks are placed on queues. Workers lease tasks from queues, run them and report the result. A schedule enqueues tasks at fixed times using cron expressions. A workflow links tasks into a directed acyclic graph.

Larkspur ships as a single binary called `lark` that contains the server, the worker runtime and the command line client.

title: Installation
text:
# Installation

Larkspur runs on Linux (kernel 4.18 or later) and macOS 12 or later. Windows is supported only through WSL2.

## Package managers

On macOS run `brew install larkspur`. On Debian and Ubuntu add the Larkspur apt repository and run `apt install larkspur`.

## Docker

The official image is `larkspur/larkspur:2.3`. Mount a volume at `/var/lib/larkspur` to persist data.

## Ports

The server listens on port 7420 by default for both the REST API and worker connections. Change it with the `port` setting in the `[server]` section or the `LARKSPUR_PORT` environment variable.

title: Quickstart
text:
# Quickstart

1. Run `lark init` to create a default configuration file and data directory.
2. Start the server with `lark server`.
3. In another terminal start a worker with `lark worker --queues default`.
4. Enqueue a test task with `lark task enqueue hello --payload '{"name": "world"}'`.

The task appears in the dashboard at http://localhost:7420/ui within a second. Use `lark task list` to see its state change from queued to running to succeeded.

title: Configuration file
text:
# Configuration file

Larkspur reads a TOML file named `larkspur.toml`. By default it looks for the file at `/etc/larkspur/larkspur.toml`. Set the `LARKSPUR_CONFIG` environment variable to use a different path.

## Sections

- `[server]` controls the listen address, port and TLS.
- `[storage]` selects the storage backend and its connection string.
- `[workers]` sets default concurrency, heartbeat interval and lease duration.
- `[logging]` sets the log level and format.

Unknown keys are rejected at startup so that typos do not go unnoticed. Run `lark config check` to validate a file without starting the server.

title: Environment variables
text:
# Environment variables

Every configuration key can be overridden with an environment variable. Environment variables take precedence over values in `larkspur.toml`.

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `LARKSPUR_PORT` | `7420` | Listen port |
| `LARKSPUR_LOG_LEVEL` | `info` | Log level |
| `LARKSPUR_DATA_DIR` | `/var/lib/larkspur` | Data directory for the embedded store |
| `LARKSPUR_CONFIG` | `/etc/larkspur/larkspur.toml` | Configuration file path |
| `LARKSPUR_TOKEN` | unset | API token used by the CLI |

title: Workers
text:
# Workers

A worker process connects to the server and executes tasks from one or more queues. Start one with `lark worker --queues default,emails`.

## Concurrency

By default a worker runs as many tasks in parallel as the machine has CPU cores. Override it with `--concurrency` or the `concurrency` key in the `[workers]` section.

## Heartbeats

Workers send a heartbeat to the server every 10 seconds. A worker that misses three consecutive heartbeats, which is 30 seconds with the default interval, is considered dead, and the tasks it had leased are returned to their queues.

title: Retries and backoff
text:
# Retries and backoff

When a task raises an error or times out, Larkspur retries it. By default a task is attempted up to 5 times in total (`max_attempts = 5`).

The delay between attempts grows exponentially: it starts at 2 seconds and doubles after every failure, up to a cap of 10 minutes. A random jitter of plus or minus 20 percent is applied so that many failing tasks do not retry at the same instant.

Set `max_attempts = 1` to disable retries for a task. When a task exhausts all of its attempts it is moved to the dead-letter queue.

title: Dead-letter queue
text:
# Dead-letter queue

Tasks that fail on their final attempt are moved to a special queue named `_dlq`. Dead-lettered tasks keep their payload, their error messages and the full attempt history.

Tasks are retained in the dead-letter queue for 14 days, after which they are deleted. Change the retention with `dlq_retention` in the `[storage]` section.

To run dead-lettered tasks again use `lark dlq replay --queue emails`. Replayed tasks start over with a fresh attempt counter.

title: Scheduling
text:
# Scheduling

Schedules enqueue a task on a recurring basis using cron expressions. Larkspur accepts standard five-field cron expressions and an optional sixth leading field for seconds.

Cron schedules are evaluated in UTC by default. Set `schedule_tz` on a schedule, for example `schedule_tz = "Asia/Kolkata"`, to evaluate it in another time zone; daylight saving transitions are handled automatically.

If the server was down when a schedule should have fired, the missed run is skipped unless `catch_up = true` is set.

title: Task priorities
text:
# Task priorities

Each task has an integer priority from 0 to 9, where 9 is the highest priority and 0 is the lowest. Tasks without an explicit priority get the default priority of 5.

Workers always lease the highest-priority task available on their queues. To prevent starvation, a queued task's effective priority is increased by one for every 60 seconds it waits, up to a maximum of 9.

title: Rate limiting
text:
# Rate limiting

Queues can be rate limited to protect downstream services. Limits use a token bucket per queue.

Set `rate_limit = "100/s"` on a queue to allow at most 100 task starts per second. Supported units are per second, per minute and per hour. The optional `burst` setting allows short bursts above the steady rate; it defaults to the per-second rate.

Rate limits are enforced cluster-wide, not per worker.

title: Timeouts
text:
# Timeouts

Every task has an execution timeout. The default task timeout is 300 seconds (five minutes). Set `timeout` on the task definition to change it.

When a task exceeds its timeout the worker first sends a soft timeout signal (SIGTERM on Unix) so that the task can clean up. If the task is still running after a 30 second grace period it is killed. A timed-out task counts as a failed attempt and is retried according to its retry policy.

title: Idempotency keys
text:
# Idempotency keys

Clients can attach an idempotency key to an enqueue request with the `Idempotency-Key` HTTP header or the `idempotency_key` SDK argument.

If another task with the same key was enqueued within the deduplication window, Larkspur returns the existing task instead of creating a new one. The deduplication window is 24 hours.

Keys are scoped to a queue, so the same key may be reused on different queues.

title: Workflows
text:
# Workflows

Workflows compose tasks into a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Larkspur supports three building blocks:

- A chain runs tasks one after another, passing each result to the next task.
- A group runs tasks in parallel.
- A chord runs a group and then a callback task once every member has finished.

Use `depends_on` to declare arbitrary dependencies. A single workflow may contain at most 10,000 tasks. If any task in a workflow fails permanently, its downstream tasks are cancelled.

title: Storage backends
text:
# Storage backends

Larkspur stores queues, tasks and results in a pluggable backend selected in the `[storage]` section.

- **embedded** (default): a log-structured store in the data directory. Ideal for single-node deployments and development.
- **postgres**: PostgreSQL 13 or newer. Recommended for production and required for clustering with more than three nodes.
- **redis**: Redis 6.2 or newer can be used as a broker for queues but cannot store task results.

Migrating between backends is done with `lark storage migrate --to postgres`.

title: Clustering
text:
# Clustering

Several Larkspur servers can form a cluster for high availability. Cluster membership and leader election use the Raft consensus protocol.

Always run an odd number of nodes; three or five nodes are recommended. A cluster of n nodes tolerates the failure of (n - 1) / 2 nodes, so a three-node cluster survives one failure and a five-node cluster survives two.

Join a node with `lark cluster join <address>`. All nodes must run the same minor version, except during a rolling upgrade.

title: TLS
text:
# TLS

Enable TLS in the `[server.tls]` section by setting `cert_file` and `key_file`. The minimum supported version is TLS 1.2; TLS 1.3 is preferred when the client supports it.

For mutual TLS set `client_ca_file`; workers and clients must then present a certificate signed by that CA. Certificates are reloaded automatically when the files change, so certificate rotation does not require a restart.

title: Authentication and roles
text:
# Authentication and roles

All API requests must carry a bearer token. Create tokens with `lark token create --role operator --name ci`.

Larkspur has three built-in roles:

- **viewer** can read queues, tasks and metrics.
- **operator** can additionally enqueue, cancel and replay tasks.
- **admin** can additionally manage tokens, schedules and cluster membership.

Tokens can be given an expiry with `--expires-in 30d`. Revoke a token with `lark token revoke <id>`.

title: REST API
text:
# REST API

The REST API is served under the base path `/api/v2`.

- `POST /api/v2/tasks` enqueues a task.
- `GET /api/v2/tasks/{id}` returns a task and its result.
- `DELETE /api/v2/tasks/{id}` cancels a queued task.
- `GET /api/v2/queues` lists queues with their depth.

List endpoints use cursor pagination. Pass the `next_cursor` value from one response as the `cursor` parameter of the next request. The maximum page size is 500 items. Errors are returned as JSON objects with `code` and `message` fields.

title: Webhooks
text:
# Webhooks

Larkspur can call your HTTP endpoint when task events happen. Supported events are `task.succeeded`, `task.failed` and `task.dead`.

Each webhook request is signed with HMAC-SHA256 using the webhook's secret. The signature is sent in the `X-Larkspur-Signature` header; verify it before trusting the payload.

If your endpoint does not return a 2xx status, delivery is retried three times with increasing delays.

title: Metrics and monitoring
text:
# Metrics and monitoring

Larkspur exposes Prometheus metrics at the `/metrics` endpoint on port 9464. The port is separate from the API port so that it can be firewalled independently.

Important metrics include:

- `larkspur_queue_depth` - tasks waiting per queue.
- `larkspur_task_duration_seconds` - histogram of task run times.
- `larkspur_task_failures_total` - failed attempts per task name.

A ready-made Grafana dashboard is published with every release.

title: Logging
text:
# Logging

The server and workers write structured JSON logs to standard output by default. Set `log_format = "text"` in the `[logging]` section for human-readable logs during development.

Supported log levels are debug, info, warn and error; the default is info. Each log line for a task includes the task id, queue and attempt number so logs can be correlated across workers.

title: Python SDK
text:
# Python SDK

Install the Python client with `pip install larkspur-client`. It supports Python 3.9 and newer.

Define tasks with the `@task` decorator and enqueue them with `.delay()`:

```python
from larkspur import Client, task

client = Client("http://localhost:7420", token="...")

@task(queue="emails", max_attempts=3)
def send_welcome(user_id: int) -> None:
    ...

send_welcome.delay(42)
```

Run workers for Python tasks with `larkspur-worker myapp.tasks`.

title: JavaScript SDK
Backups
text:
# Backups

For the embedded store, create an online backup with `lark backup create --out /backups/lark.snap`. Backups are consistent snapshots and can be taken while the server is running.

Restore a snapshot with `lark backup restore --from /backups/lark.snap` while the server is stopped.

When using the postgres backend, back up the database with the usual PostgreSQL tools such as `pg_dump`; `lark backup` is not needed.

title: Upgrading
text:
# Upgrading

Upgrades within the same major version can be done as rolling upgrades: upgrade one node at a time and wait for it to rejoin the cluster. Do not skip more than one minor version in a single upgrade.

Upgrading from 1.x to 2.x is a major upgrade. It requires downtime: stop all nodes, run `lark migrate` against the data directory or database, and then start the new version. Read the 2.0 release notes before upgrading.

title: Release notes 2.0
text:
# Larkspur 2.0 release notes

## New

- Workflows with chains, groups, chords and arbitrary DAG dependencies.
- REST API v2 under `/api/v2` with cursor pagination.
- Role-based access control with viewer, operator and admin roles.

## Breaking changes

- The XML-RPC API was removed; use the REST API instead.
- The configuration format changed from YAML to TOML.
- Upgrading from 1.x requires running `lark migrate`.

title: Release notes 2.3
text:
# Larkspur 2.3 release notes

## New

- Rate limits gained a `burst` setting.
- Webhook signatures now use HMAC-SHA256 (previously HMAC-SHA1).
- The Python SDK supports Python 3.13.
- `lark task inspect` shows the full attempt history of a task.

## Deprecations

- `lark queue purge --all` is deprecated and will be removed in 3.0; purge queues individually instead.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
# Troubleshooting

## A task is stuck in the reserved state

A task stays reserved while a worker holds its lease. If the worker crashed, the lease expires after the visibility timeout, which is 60 seconds by default, and the task returns to its queue. Use `lark task inspect <id>` to see which worker holds the lease.

## Workers cannot connect

Check that the server port (7420 by default) is reachable and that the worker uses a valid token. With mutual TLS enabled, the worker certificate must be signed by the configured client CA.

title: Limits
text:
# Limits

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Maximum task payload size | 1 MiB |
| Maximum queue name length | 64 characters |
| Default result retention | 7 days |
| Maximum tasks per workflow | 10,000 |
| Maximum API page size | 500 |

Payloads larger than 1 MiB should be stored externally, for example in object storage, and passed by reference.
